16920:
Uttermost means the absolute greatest, highest, or farthest point possible — with nothing beyond it.

Think of it as a wall at the very end of everything. You cannot go further than the uttermost point. You cannot exceed the uttermost degree. It marks the final, extreme limit — of a distance, an effort, an emotion, or a quality.

The adjective "uttermost" works in two related but distinct ways:

1. The Greatest Possible Degree (of something abstract)

This is the most common use. It describes qualities, efforts, feelings, or states pushed to their absolute maximum — where nothing more is left to give or reach.

"The surgeon worked with uttermost precision."
"She treated the matter with uttermost seriousness."
"He was in uttermost despair."

In these sentences, "uttermost" means there is no higher level of precision, seriousness, or despair imaginable. The word carries enormous weight — it tells you that the thing being described is not just great, but maxed out completely.

2. The Farthest Possible Distance (physical or figurative)

"Uttermost" also describes the extreme edge of a physical or conceptual space — the remotest, most distant point you can reach.

"Missionaries travelled to the uttermost parts of the earth."
"Light from the uttermost corners of the universe takes billions of years to reach us."

Here, "uttermost" means the very last frontier — beyond which there is simply nothing more. It conjures a sense of vast, almost unreachable remoteness.

"Uttermost" is not a neutral word. It carries strong emotional and dramatic weight. When someone uses it, they are deliberately choosing the most intense, absolute version of what they want to say. It leaves no room for exaggeration — it is the exaggeration, taken to its logical end.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "He tried hard."
  • "He tried with uttermost effort."

The second sentence tells you that every drop of effort was used up. Nothing was held back.

Uttermost is a formal, literary word. You are unlikely to hear someone say it in casual conversation. It belongs to writing, speeches, religious texts, literature, and solemn contexts. The Bible, for example, uses it frequently — "the uttermost parts of the earth" — and this has given the word a certain majestic, serious tone that has stuck to it over centuries.

If you used it in everyday conversation, it would sound deliberately dramatic or old-fashioned. That is not wrong — sometimes that weight is exactly what a writer or speaker wants.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding a word also means knowing how it sits next to its neighbors:

  • Utmost — This is the modern, everyday version of the same idea. "Uttermost" and "utmost" mean the same thing, but "utmost" is far more common today. Think of "uttermost" as the grander, more ceremonial sibling.
  • Extreme — Means very far from the centre or norm, but doesn't quite insist on being the absolute final limit the way "uttermost" does.
  • Ultimate — Means the last or final in a sequence. "Uttermost" focuses more on degree and distance than on being the last in a series.
  • Outermost — Refers only to physical position (the farthest layer or edge). "Uttermost" can do this too, but it also reaches into abstract qualities, which "outermost" cannot.

The simplest way to remember "uttermost" is this:

Uttermost = the absolute limit. Nothing more exists beyond it.

Whether you are talking about the farthest point in space, the deepest possible sorrow, the greatest imaginable care, or the highest level of skill — "uttermost" places whatever you are describing at the very edge of what is possible, with a wall behind it saying: this is as far as it goes.

It is a word of totality, gravity, and finality. Use it when you want to communicate that something has reached its absolute ceiling — and that ceiling is high.
16921:
Uxorial means "of, relating to, or characteristic of a wife." Whenever something is described as uxorial, it belongs to, comes from, or is typical of a wife — her role, her behavior, her feelings, or her position within a marriage.

A useful parallel: just as "maternal" means relating to a mother and "paternal" means relating to a father, uxorial means relating to a wife. It uses the wife as the central reference point.
What this looks like in practice

In a sentence like "She fulfilled her uxorial duties with grace," uxorial simply means the duties that come with being a wife. In "His will reflected deep uxorial affection," it means affection directed toward or associated with his wife. In "She shed her uxorial identity after the divorce," it means her identity as a wife. In every case, the word is just pointing you back to the wife — her role, her experience, her status.

Importantly, uxorial is a neutral word. It carries no praise or criticism on its own. It doesn't say whether a wife's role is good or bad, important or trivial. It simply points to the wife as the reference point.

This is the single most important distinction to learn. There's a closely related word, uxorious (ending in "-ious" instead of "-ial"), and the two are frequently mixed up. Uxorious describes a husband who is excessively, even weakly, devoted to his wife — a man who submits to her every wish to a degree that others might find embarrassing or ridiculous. It carries a gently mocking, slightly negative tone.

The split is clean: uxorial describes things relating to a wife (neutral descriptor), while uxorious describes a husband who is overly doting (subtly critical). One is about the wife; the other is about how a husband behaves toward her.
Who uses this word, and where

Uxorial is a formal, literary word — you will never hear it at a dinner table or in casual conversation. It lives in legal documents (discussing a wife's rights, duties, or entitlements in historical or formal contexts), in academic writing about marriage in sociology, anthropology, and history, and in literary or classic fiction. If you use it correctly in writing, it immediately signals a precise and sophisticated vocabulary.

Uxorial is not about women in general, or about female partners broadly. It is specifically about a wife — a woman in the formal, recognized role of marriage. The word carries that institutional weight.

Every single time you see or hear the word uxorial, just think: "This is about the wife." Her role. Her duties. Her feelings. Her position. The word is simply the adjective that belongs to her. That one sentence captures everything the word does.
16922:
Uxorious describes a husband who is excessively devoted, submissive, or indulgent toward his wife — so much so that it becomes a weakness or a flaw.

The single most important word in that definition is excessively. Normal love, care, and devotion toward a wife do not make someone uxorious. What makes a man uxorious is when that devotion crosses a line into something foolish, blind, or embarrassing — when he cannot say no to her, always puts her wishes above everything else (including his own judgment, dignity, or responsibilities), and is essentially controlled by her without even realising it.

Think of it on a scale:

  • Loving husband → good, healthy, normal.
  • Very devoted husband → still fine, admirable even.
  • Uxorious husband → gone too far. He has become so wrapped up in pleasing his wife that he has lost his own spine, judgment, or independence.

The uxorious husband isn't just in love. He is weak in his love. He is blind in it. He will do whatever his wife says, agree with whatever she thinks, and prioritise her every whim even when it's unreasonable.

This word carries a mildly negative and sometimes gently mocking tone. When someone calls a man uxorious, they are not complimenting him. They are suggesting, with a slightly raised eyebrow, that he is under his wife's thumb — perhaps even that she runs the show and he simply obeys.

That said, it isn't a harsh insult. It's more of a sophisticated, literary way of pointing out a man's excessive softness toward his wife. In some contexts, it can even be used humorously — almost with affection — to describe a man who is charmingly, absurdly devoted.
Who Does This Word Apply To?

This is important: uxorious is a gendered, specific word. It applies only to a husband and his relationship with his wife. You would not use it to describe:

  • A wife being overly devoted to her husband (there are other words for that).
  • A boyfriend and girlfriend.
  • A general love between any two people.

It is specifically about a married man being excessively submissive or indulgent toward his wife. That specificity is part of what makes the word so precise and useful.

These sentences will show you exactly how the word feels in real use:

"He was so uxorious that he cancelled his own surgery to attend his wife's book club dinner."

Here, the excess is clear — skipping medical care for a trivial social event of his wife's is beyond devotion; it is foolishness.

"His friends had stopped inviting him out, knowing his uxorious nature meant he would never come without first getting his wife's approval — and she would never give it."

Here, the uxorious quality has made him socially weak and dependent.

"The king was uxorious to a ruinous degree; he reversed sound laws and appointed unqualified ministers simply because his wife asked him to."

Here, the uxoriousness has real consequences — it leads to bad decisions and harm.

"He smiled at being called uxorious. 'If loving my wife too much is a flaw,' he said, 'I'll live with it.'"

Here, the word is used more gently and humorously, and the man brushes it off as a playful accusation.

Because the word is easy to misuse, it helps to know what it does not mean:

  • It does not simply mean "a man who loves his wife." That is just being a good husband.
  • It does not mean a man who respects his wife's opinion. That is healthy partnership.
  • It does not mean a man who is kind or generous to his wife. That is normal decency.

You need that excess — the loss of independent judgment, the foolishness, the submission — for the word to apply correctly.

The noun form of this word is uxoriousness — meaning the quality or state of being uxorious.

"His uxoriousness was well known around town."
When Would You Actually See This Word?

Uxorious is a formal and somewhat old-fashioned word. You are unlikely to hear it in casual everyday conversation. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic or literary fiction (19th and early 20th century novels in particular).
  • Formal essays or critiques, especially about historical figures or characters.
  • Vocabulary enrichment contexts — word-of-the-day lists, crossword puzzles, advanced dictionaries.
  • Humorous or elevated writing, where a writer reaches for a precise, slightly archaic word to paint a vivid picture of a submissive husband.

If you had to remember just one thing:

Uxorious = a husband who is excessively and weakly devoted to his wife, to a degree that goes beyond love into foolishness or submissiveness.

That's it. Loving your wife is beautiful. Being uxorious is loving her so much, and so blindly, that you lose your own judgment in the process.
16923:
A vacancy is an empty space, position, or slot that is available to be filled.

The key thing to understand is this: a vacancy is not just any emptiness — it is a specific kind of emptiness. It is a gap where something or someone belongs, or where something or someone could be placed. Think of it like an empty seat at a dinner table that has already been set with a plate and cutlery. The seat is empty, yes — but it is clearly waiting to be occupied.

This is what separates "vacancy" from just saying something is "empty." A vacancy carries the sense of a space meant to be filled.

Vacancy is used in a few distinct but closely related ways:

1. A Job or Position That Is Unfilled

This is one of the most common uses. When an organization has a vacancy, it means there is an open role or position that nobody currently holds — and the organization is usually looking for someone to fill it.

  • "There is a vacancy in our marketing team." → One job role in the marketing team has no one doing it right now.
  • "She applied for the vacancy advertised in the newspaper." → She applied for the open job that was posted.
  • "The vacancy arose because the previous manager retired." → The position became open when someone left.

Notice that the word implies the role exists and needs to be filled — it's not that the job never existed; it's that the seat is currently empty.

2. An Unoccupied Room, House, or Property

In the context of housing, hotels, or real estate, a vacancy means a room, apartment, or property that is currently unoccupied and available.

  • "The hotel had no vacancies." → Every room was taken; none were available.
  • "The landlord had a vacancy on the third floor." → One apartment on the third floor had no tenant living in it.
  • "The motel sign flashed 'Vacancy,' so we stopped for the night." → Rooms were available.

You have surely seen the classic roadside motel signs that say "Vacancy" or "No Vacancy." This is exactly this sense — it tells travelers whether rooms are available or not.

3. The State or Condition of Being Unoccupied

More broadly, vacancy can refer to the state of something being empty or unoccupied — not just a single empty slot, but the overall condition of emptiness.

  • "The vacancy of the old building gave it an eerie feeling." → The building was empty and unoccupied, and this gave it a certain atmosphere.
  • "There is a high rate of vacancy in office buildings downtown." → Many offices are currently unoccupied.

Here, the word describes a situation rather than pointing to a specific single gap.

4. Emptiness of Mind — A Blank, Thoughtless State

This is a slightly more literary or formal use, but an important one. Vacancy can describe a state of mental blankness — when someone's mind appears completely empty, unfocused, or absent of thought.

  • "He stared out the window with an expression of complete vacancy." → His face showed no thought, no emotion — just a blank, empty look.
  • "Her eyes held a strange vacancy, as though she wasn't really present." → She had a distant, unfocused look, as if her mind was somewhere else entirely.

You might also see the adjective form "vacant" used this way: "a vacant stare" or "a vacant look."
The Important Nuance: Not All Emptiness Is a Vacancy

This is worth repeating because it sharpens your understanding significantly.

A vacancy always implies a slot, role, space, or structure that is designed to hold something — and that thing is currently missing.

  • The sky is empty at night — but we would not call the sky a "vacancy."
  • A glass with no water is empty — but we would not call it a "vacancy."
  • But a job position with no one doing it? That is a vacancy. A hotel room with no guest? A vacancy. A seat on a committee with no member filling it? A vacancy.

The word always carries the sense that something is missing from a place where it belongs or could belong.

These are natural word combinations you will often see with "vacancy":

  • Fill a vacancy — to find someone or something to occupy the empty position. "They are looking to fill the vacancy quickly."
  • Job vacancy / employment vacancy — an open position at a workplace.
  • Post a vacancy — to advertise an open job. "The company posted the vacancy on its website."
  • A vacancy arises / occurs — when a position becomes empty, usually because someone left. "A vacancy arose when the director resigned."
  • No Vacancy — seen on signs, meaning no rooms or spaces are available.
  • Vacancy rate — used in business and real estate to describe what percentage of rooms or properties are unoccupied at a given time.

SenseWhat it means

To put it all together simply: vacancy means an empty position, space, or slot that is available or waiting to be filled — whether that is a job, a hotel room, an apartment, or even a person's mind. The word always carries the feeling of a gap, an absence, something missing from a place where it naturally belongs. When something or someone fills that gap, the vacancy disappears.
16924:
"Vacant" means not occupied — it describes a space, a position, or even a person's expression that has nothing or no one in it, or that shows no thought or feeling at all.

The one thread running through every use of this word is this: something is there, but nothing — or no one — is filling it.
Sense 1: A Physical Space with No Person Occupying It

The most common everyday use of "vacant" describes a physical place that no one is currently using or living in.

When you walk into a cinema and see a seat nobody is sitting in, that seat is vacant. When a hotel has rooms available because no guests are checked in, those rooms are vacant. When you walk past a house with no furniture inside, no lights on, and nobody living there, that house is vacant. A patch of land in a city where no building stands — nobody's shop, nobody's home — is called a vacant lot.

The word works for smaller spaces too. A vacant parking spot is one no car is occupying. A vacant desk in an office is one no one is working at.
Sense 2: A Job or Role That Nobody Currently Holds

"Vacant" is also used for jobs, positions, or official roles that are open and waiting to be filled. If a company's marketing director just quit, the director's position is now vacant — nobody holds it, and it needs to be filled.

This is why job advertisements sometimes carry the phrase "Position Vacant" — it's a formal way of saying: this role exists, but no one is doing it yet. A committee with three unfilled spots has three vacant seats. A throne that no one is ruling from is vacant.
Sense 3: A Face, Eyes, or Look Showing No Thought or Awareness

This is perhaps the most vivid sense of "vacant." When applied to a person's face, eyes, or expression, it means completely blank — showing no sign of thought, emotion, or real awareness. The person is physically present, but their mind seems to be somewhere else entirely.

A vacant stare is one where the eyes are open and pointed in a direction, but there is clearly nothing going on behind them — no recognition, no feeling, no engagement. If someone asks you a question and you respond with a vacant smile, you are smiling without any real understanding of what was said. After a long, exhausting journey, a person might sit with a vacant look on their face — dazed, zoned out, not really taking anything in.

A useful way to picture it: the lights are on, but nobody's home.

These two words are close cousins, and learners often wonder when to use which.

Empty is the broader, more general word. It simply means "containing nothing." A glass with no water in it is empty. A box with nothing inside it is empty. The street was empty in the early morning.

Vacant is more specific. It almost always refers to a space, a seat, or a role that could be occupied by a person (or filled by someone taking on a position), but currently isn't. It carries the quiet implication of potential — a place ready and waiting.

Because of this, you would say a hotel room is vacant, not just empty. You would say a job position is vacant, not empty. You would say a stare is vacant, not empty. But you would say a cup is empty, not vacant — because a cup is not meant to be "occupied" by a person.

The simplest test: if the thing you are describing is meant to hold a person or a person's role, "vacant" is almost always the right choice over "empty."

Knowing the natural word pairings helps you use the word correctly and confidently.

For physical spaces, the most natural pairings are: a vacant seat, a vacant chair, a vacant room, a vacant apartment, a vacant house, a vacant building, a vacant lot, vacant land, and a vacant parking spot.

For jobs and roles, you will see: a vacant position, a vacant post, a vacant role, and a vacant seat (on a board or committee).

For expressions and looks: a vacant stare, a vacant look, a vacant expression, a vacant gaze, a vacant smile, and vacant eyes.
Related Word Forms You Will Encounter

Vacancy (noun) is the noun form of "vacant." It refers either to the state of being vacant, or to a specific instance of something being empty and available. A hotel with rooms available has vacancies. A company looking to fill an open job has a vacancy. The famous motel sign "No Vacancy" means all rooms are taken.

Vacate (verb) means to leave a place, thereby making it vacant. "Guests must vacate their rooms by 11 AM." When you vacate a space, you leave it and make it available for others.

Vacantly (adverb) describes doing something in a vacant way — blankly, without real awareness or engagement. "She stared vacantly out the window, lost in her own world."

No matter how "vacant" is used, the core meaning stays the same: a space, role, or mind that is unoccupied. Something is there — a seat, a building, a job, a pair of eyes — but no one is filling it.

In its most concrete sense, it means a physical place with no one in it. In its professional sense, it means a job with no one doing it. In its most human and expressive sense, it describes a face or gaze that shows a person who is present in body, but absent in mind.
16925: "Vacate" means to leave something and make it empty or available. Whether it's a physical place, a job position, or a legal ruling — when someone vacates something, they move out of it, give it up, or clear it away. The word always carries the idea of removal and making something no longer occupied or in force.

This is the most everyday use of the word. To vacate a place means to physically leave it and stop occupying it, usually so that the space becomes empty or available for someone else.

"Guests must vacate their hotel rooms by noon."
"The protesters were ordered to vacate the building."
"We had to vacate the apartment at the end of the lease."

Notice that "vacate" is slightly more formal and official-sounding than simply saying "leave." When someone says "leave the room," it's casual. When someone says "vacate the room," it implies an obligation, a rule, or an official instruction. You'll often hear it from authority figures — hotel managers, landlords, police officers, judges — telling someone they must clear out of a space.

A very common phrase is "vacate the premises." "Premises" means a building and the land it sits on, so "vacate the premises" simply means to leave the property entirely. It sounds very formal, and it usually is — it's the kind of phrase you'd see in a legal notice or hear from law enforcement.
Meaning 2: To Give Up a Position, Role, or Seat

"Vacate" is also used when someone leaves a job, an office, a post, or any kind of role they hold. Here, the idea is not about a physical space, but about a position of responsibility or authority. When someone vacates a position, they step down from it or leave it empty for the next person.

"The CEO vacated her position after the merger."
"The senator vacated his seat before the end of his term."
"Two judges vacated their posts, leaving the court understaffed."

This usage is common in formal, political, or professional writing. You would rarely say this in casual speech — in everyday conversation, you'd more likely say "quit," "step down from," or "leave" a job. But in newspapers, official documents, or professional settings, "vacate" fits naturally.
Meaning 3: To Officially Cancel or Set Aside (Legal Use)

This is a distinct and very important meaning used in law and courts. When a judge or court vacates a ruling, a judgment, a conviction, or an order, they officially cancel it — they declare that it is no longer valid and has no legal effect. This is different from simply disagreeing with a ruling; vacating it means wiping it away as if it were undone.

"The appeals court vacated the defendant's conviction."
"The judge vacated the earlier order and issued a new one."
"His sentence was vacated after new evidence emerged."

If someone's conviction is vacated, for example, it means the court has officially annulled that conviction — the person is no longer legally considered to have been convicted of that crime. Think of it as the court pressing an "undo" button on a legal decision.

This meaning is very specific to legal and official contexts. Outside of courtrooms and legal documents, you would not use "vacate" this way.

Leave is the most general word. You can "leave" anywhere, anytime, for any reason, casually or formally. "Vacate" is much more specific — it implies you are required to leave, or that leaving has a formal/official significance.

Evacuate means to leave urgently because of danger (a fire, a flood, a disaster). "Vacate" does not carry urgency or emergency. You vacate a hotel room calmly at checkout; you evacuate a building when there's a fire.

Abandon means to leave something behind permanently, often irresponsibly or without care. "Vacate" is neutral and orderly — there's no negative judgment attached. Vacating a place is simply leaving it properly.

Annul / Overturn / Reverse are related to the legal meaning of vacate, but each has its own shade. To overturn or reverse a ruling means to replace it with the opposite decision. To annul something is to declare it was never valid to begin with. To vacate is specifically to cancel and set aside — often without immediately replacing the ruling, though a new ruling may follow.

"Vacate" is a formal word. It is most at home in legal documents, official notices, professional writing, and formal speech. It wouldn't sound natural in casual conversation. You would not normally say to a friend, "I vacated my apartment." You would say, "I moved out of my apartment." But in a legal notice to a tenant, "You are required to vacate the premises by Friday" is perfectly standard.
Quick Summary of All Three Uses

To put it plainly:

1. You vacate a place → you leave it and make it empty. (Vacate the room, vacate the building, vacate the premises.)

2. You vacate a position → you step down or move out of a role. (Vacate a seat, vacate an office, vacate a post.)

3. A court vacates a ruling → the ruling is officially cancelled and has no legal force. (Vacate a conviction, vacate an order, vacate a judgment.)

In all three cases, the underlying idea is the same: something that was occupied, held, or in force is now emptied, given up, or removed. That's the soul of the word "vacate."
16926:
To vaccinate someone means to put a special substance called a vaccine into their body — almost always through a needle (an injection/shot) — so that their body learns how to fight a specific disease before they ever actually get it.

Think of it this way: you are giving the body a practice run against a disease, so that if the real disease ever shows up, the body is already prepared to defeat it quickly.

When a doctor or nurse vaccinates you, the vaccine goes into your body and "shows" your immune system what the disease looks like. The immune system then builds special weapons called antibodies against it. These antibodies stay in your body. So later, if the real disease tries to infect you, your immune system recognizes it immediately and fights it off — often so fast that you don't even get sick.

You are not being given the disease itself (at least not in a form that can harm you). You are being given a safe signal that teaches your body what to prepare for.

Vaccinate is a transitive verb, meaning it always acts on someone or something. You vaccinate a person or an animal. You never just "vaccinate" in the air — there must be a receiver of the action.

The standard pattern is:

Vaccinate + [person/animal] + against + [disease]

This is the most natural and complete structure. The word "against" is almost always the preposition paired with this verb because vaccination is an act of defense — you vaccinate against something threatening.

Here are examples showing how the verb works in different forms:

Active voice (someone does the vaccinating):

  • The nurse vaccinated the child against polio.
  • The government plans to vaccinate millions of people against the flu this winter.
  • The vet vaccinated all the dogs against rabies.

Passive voice (the focus is on who received the vaccine):

  • The child was vaccinated against polio last Tuesday.
  • Millions of people have been vaccinated against COVID-19.
  • All travelers must be vaccinated against yellow fever before entering the country.

With "get" (very common in everyday speech):

  • You should get vaccinated before your trip abroad.
  • Have you gotten vaccinated yet?

Reflexive / general use:

  • Countries that vaccinated their populations early saw fewer deaths.
  • Parents are encouraged to vaccinate their children on schedule.

It is important to know what the word does not cover:

  • It does not mean simply giving someone medicine through a needle. If a nurse injects you with a painkiller, that is not vaccinating — because the purpose is not to build immunity against a disease.
  • It does not mean treating a disease you already have. If you are already sick and a doctor gives you treatment, that is not vaccinating — vaccination is always preventive (before the disease arrives), not curative (after you are already ill).
  • It does not guarantee 100% protection in all cases. Vaccines greatly reduce the risk and severity of disease, but some vaccines are more effective than others, and some people may still get a mild version of the illness.

When you say someone was vaccinated, it implies they received protection — but how strong and how long that protection lasts depends entirely on the specific vaccine:

  • Some vaccines (like the one for smallpox) provide lifelong protection from just one or two doses.
  • Others (like the flu vaccine) need to be given every year because the disease keeps changing.
  • Some require multiple doses over time, called a vaccination series, to build full protection (e.g., the hepatitis B vaccine).

When a person needs to be vaccinated again after some time, it is called a booster shot — because it "boosts" (strengthens) the immunity that may have faded.

The subject of the verb (the one doing the vaccinating) is typically:

  • A doctor, nurse, or healthcare worker in a clinical setting
  • A veterinarian (for animals)
  • A government or health authority (in broader, policy-level language: "The country vaccinated 80% of its population.")

The object (the one being vaccinated) is typically:

  • A person (a child, a patient, a traveler, the elderly)
  • An animal (a pet, livestock, wildlife in conservation programs)

Since you are learning the verb, it helps to see how it connects to the words around it:

FormWordExample
VerbvaccinateDoctors vaccinate children every year.
Noun (the act)vaccinationVaccination saves millions of lives.
Noun (the substance)vaccineThe vaccine was stored in a cold refrigerator.
AdjectivevaccinatedOnly vaccinated passengers were allowed to board.
Adjective (opposite)unvaccinatedUnvaccinated people faced a higher risk.

To vaccinate is one of the most important words in the field of medicine and public health. It describes one of humanity's greatest achievements — a method of tricking the immune system (in a safe way) into preparing itself for a dangerous enemy it has not yet faced. Diseases like smallpox have been completely wiped off the planet, and diseases like polio and measles have been dramatically reduced — all because of the act of vaccinating populations on a wide scale.

So in the simplest possible summary:

To vaccinate = to give someone a vaccine so their body learns to protect itself against a specific disease, before that disease ever attacks.
16927: Vaccination is the act of giving a person (or animal) a vaccine — a specially prepared substance — to protect them from a specific disease. The goal is to make the body ready to fight that disease before it ever actually encounters it.
The core idea: teaching your immune system

Your body has an immune system — a natural defense force that fights off germs like viruses and bacteria. When you catch a disease for the first time, your immune system fights it, but this takes time. During that time, you get sick, sometimes seriously.

Vaccination is a way to train your immune system in advance, without you having to go through the actual disease.

A vaccine introduces something into your body — it could be a weakened or killed version of a germ, a small harmless piece of it, or even just a set of chemical instructions — that teaches your immune system what that germ looks like. Your body then builds antibodies: specialized proteins that know how to target and destroy that specific germ.

If the real germ ever enters your body in the future, your immune system already knows it. It responds fast, often before you even get sick — or at least makes the illness much milder.

The word can refer to:

  • A single event: "The vaccination took only a few seconds." (meaning: the moment a vaccine was administered)
  • The overall process or practice: "Vaccination has saved millions of lives." (meaning: the broader medical practice of using vaccines)
  • A program or campaign: "The government launched a vaccination drive across the country."

So depending on context, it can mean the specific act of injecting a vaccine into one person, or the entire concept of using vaccines as a public health tool.
Types of vaccination (based on how the vaccine works)

There are different kinds of vaccines, and therefore different kinds of vaccination:

  • Live-attenuated vaccination: The vaccine contains a weakened (but living) form of the germ. Example: the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
  • Inactivated vaccination: The vaccine contains a killed version of the germ. Example: some flu vaccines.
  • Subunit vaccination: Only a small, harmless piece of the germ (like a protein from its surface) is used. Example: the hepatitis B vaccine.
  • mRNA vaccination: The vaccine gives your cells temporary chemical instructions to produce a harmless protein that the immune system can learn from. Example: the COVID-19 vaccines from Pfizer and Moderna.
  • Booster vaccination: An additional dose given after the initial one(s) to "remind" or strengthen the immune system's memory. Example: tetanus boosters given every few years.

The word "vaccination" applies to all of these — the type just describes the specific method used.
Why vaccination matters: beyond the individual

Vaccination protects not just the person who receives it, but potentially everyone around them. This is through a concept called herd immunity (also called community immunity):

When a large enough share of a population is vaccinated, a disease can no longer spread easily — because it keeps running into immune people who can't pass it on. This protects vulnerable people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns, the elderly, or people with certain medical conditions.

This is why vaccination is considered one of the most important tools in public health. It has:

  • Eradicated smallpox entirely (the last natural case was in 1977)
  • Brought polio to the edge of elimination worldwide
  • Dramatically reduced deaths from measles, diphtheria, whooping cough, and many other diseases

It helps to know how "vaccination" relates to nearby words:

  • Vaccine (noun): the actual substance — the liquid or preparation that is administered. ("The doctor prepared the vaccine.")
  • Vaccinate (verb): the action of giving a vaccine to someone. ("The nurse will vaccinate the child today.")
  • Vaccination (noun): the act, process, or event of vaccinating. ("The vaccination was quick and painless.")
  • Vaccinated (adjective): describes a person or animal that has received a vaccine. ("She is fully vaccinated.")
  • Vaccinator (noun): a person who administers vaccines.

You will often see "vaccination" used with these words:

  • Routine vaccination — vaccines given as part of a standard schedule (e.g., childhood vaccines)
  • Mandatory/compulsory vaccination — vaccination required by law or policy
  • Mass vaccination — vaccinating a large population quickly, often during an outbreak
  • Vaccination campaign / drive / program — an organized effort to vaccinate many people
  • Vaccination schedule — a planned timetable of which vaccines to give and when
  • Vaccination rate — the percentage of a population that has been vaccinated
  • Childhood vaccination — vaccines administered in early life to protect children
  • Flu vaccination — specifically for influenza

• "The doctor advised annual vaccination against the flu, especially for the elderly."
  • "Mass vaccination campaigns helped bring polio to the brink of extinction."
  • "The school required proof of vaccination before enrollment."
  • "She experienced mild soreness after her vaccination, which was completely normal."
  • "Increasing vaccination rates is key to achieving herd immunity."
  • "A booster vaccination is sometimes needed when immunity fades over time."

Vaccination is the medical act or practice of introducing a vaccine into a person's body to trigger an immune response — training the body to recognize and fight a specific disease without the person having to suffer through it. It protects individuals, shields vulnerable communities through herd immunity, and at the largest scale, has helped humanity control or eliminate some of history's deadliest diseases.
16928:
To vacillate means to go back and forth between two or more choices, opinions, or positions — again and again — without being able to settle on one. It describes a kind of restless, repeated indecision.

Think of a pendulum on a clock. It swings left, then right, then left again, never stopping on either side. A person who vacillates does the same thing — but inside their mind. They lean toward Option A, then pull back toward Option B, then drift back to Option A, and so on. They can't commit. They can't land.

Vacillating is not just a single moment of "I'm not sure." It's a repeated, ongoing pattern of swinging between options. The key ingredients are:

  • Two or more sides pulling at the person
  • Movement back and forth between those sides
  • An inability to stay decided — they make up their mind, then unmake it
  • Duration — this usually happens over a period of time, not just a split second

So if you make a choice and stick with it, you are not vacillating. If you make a choice, change your mind, go back to the first choice, then change your mind again — that is vacillating.
A Vivid Example to Make It Stick

Imagine your friend is trying to decide whether to move to a new city for a job.

On Monday, she says: "I'm going to take the job! This is a great opportunity."
On Wednesday, she says: "Actually, I don't think I should leave. My family is here."
On Friday, she says: "You know what, I've thought about it more — I should go. I can't miss this."
On Sunday, she says: "I just can't do it. I'm staying."

She is vacillating — swinging back and forth between "go" and "stay," unable to make a firm, lasting decision.

You could say: "She has been vacillating about the job offer for weeks."

Vacillating often comes from a place of genuine conflict. The person can see real value on both sides, and that's exactly what makes it so hard. It's not laziness. It's a kind of mental tug-of-war where neither side fully wins.

However, from the outside, watching someone vacillate can be exhausting and frustrating — because you never know where they actually stand.
Connotation — Is It a Good or Bad Thing?

Vacillate carries a mildly negative connotation. It suggests weakness of resolve, unreliability, or an inability to lead oneself. It paints a picture of someone who can't be counted on to hold a position.

It is not the same as being thoughtfully open-minded or carefully reconsidering. Those are seen as virtues. Vacillating, on the other hand, suggests a messy, anxious, unresolved kind of going back and forth that doesn't serve the person well.

If a politician keeps changing their stance on an issue every few days, a journalist might write: "The senator has vacillated on this policy for months, leaving voters confused." That sentence is critical — it implies the senator lacks clear conviction.

Here are several examples across different situations, so you can see the word in action:

  • He vacillated between choosing medicine and law as his career for two whole years before finally enrolling in medical school.
  • Don't vacillate — make a decision and stand by it.
  • She vacillated so much that the opportunity passed before she could act.
  • The committee has been vacillating on the new policy for months.
  • I could tell he was vacillating because every time I asked him, I got a different answer.

Notice that vacillate is often followed by "between" — vacillate between X and Y — because it almost always involves two sides pulling in opposite directions.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close to vacillate in meaning, but each has its own flavour:

Hesitate means to pause before doing something. It's a single, brief moment of uncertainty. Vacillating is deeper and longer — it's repeated back-and-forth, not just a pause.

She hesitated before answering = one brief pause.
She vacillated for days about what to answer = prolonged, repeated indecision.

Waver is probably the closest synonym. To waver also means to become unsteady in a decision or belief. Vacillate and waver are often interchangeable, but vacillate tends to feel a bit more formal, and it more specifically implies a rhythmic back-and-forth movement between positions.

Dither means to be nervously indecisive, often in a flustered or ineffective way. Dithering carries a slightly more anxious, helpless, even comical tone. Vacillating sounds more serious and deliberate by comparison.

Oscillate literally means to swing back and forth (like a pendulum or a sound wave). It can be used figuratively like vacillate, but it's more commonly used in science and physics. Vacillate is specifically reserved for human indecision and opinion.

Vacillating sits in the moderate-to-strong range of indecision. It's stronger than simply "being unsure." It implies that the person has been going back and forth noticeably, likely over a meaningful period of time, and that others around them have probably noticed or been affected by it.

To make sure the word is crystal clear, here's what it does not mean:

  • It does not mean to lie or deliberately mislead. A person who vacillates is genuinely torn, not dishonest.
  • It does not mean to slowly change your mind once based on new evidence. That's called updating or reconsidering. Vacillating is about going back and forth, not a single directional shift.
  • It does not describe physical shaking or trembling in common modern usage (though an archaic meaning existed). If someone's hands are trembling, we don't say they are vacillating.

If you want to remember this word in one line:

To vacillate = to repeatedly swing back and forth between choices, unable to commit to one side.

Picture that pendulum. Picture your friend who can never decide what to order at a restaurant, leaning toward the pasta, then the salad, then back to the pasta. That is vacillating — in miniature.
16929:
Vacillation is the act of going back and forth between two or more choices, opinions, or positions — again and again — without being able to settle on one and stick with it.

Think of a person deciding whether to quit their job. Monday they think, "Yes, I'm quitting." Tuesday they think, "No, I'll stay." Wednesday, "Actually, I'll quit." Thursday, "Maybe I should stay a bit longer..." This repeated mental ping-pong, this inability to plant your flag and stand firm — that is vacillation.
The Shape of the Word's Meaning

Vacillation is not just a single moment of hesitation. It's a pattern. It implies that someone has gone back and forth multiple times, possibly over a long period. The repetition is built into the word's soul.

It also carries a slightly negative tone. When you describe someone's behavior as vacillation, you're suggesting that they should have made a decision by now, but they haven't — and that this is a weakness, not a virtue. It implies a lack of resolve, backbone, or conviction.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close neighbours, but they are not identical:

Hesitation is a pause before acting. You stand at the edge of the diving board for a moment before jumping. That's hesitation — one brief moment of uncertainty. Vacillation is much more prolonged and repeated than that.

Indecision is the general state of not being able to decide. Vacillation is more specific — it describes the motion of swinging back and forth. You can think of indecision as the condition, and vacillation as what that condition looks like in action.

Wavering is the closest synonym and is nearly interchangeable with vacillation. However, wavering can sometimes describe a single wobble in conviction ("he wavered for a moment"), while vacillation almost always implies a longer, more drawn-out pattern of back-and-forth.

Dithering is an informal word for the same idea, but it adds a flavor of fussiness and wasted time — someone who dithers is almost annoyingly indecisive. Vacillation is more formal and neutral by comparison, though still critical.

This is important for sharpening your understanding:

  • It is not simply changing your mind once. If you decided to paint your room blue, then changed it to green, that's just changing your mind. Vacillation requires the repeated back-and-forth.
  • It is not careful, thoughtful deliberation. If someone takes time to study all the options before making a well-reasoned decision, that's prudence or careful thinking — something positive. Vacillation, by contrast, suggests that the going back and forth is unproductive and driven by uncertainty or weakness of will, not by the gathering of useful new information.
  • It is not about uncertainty over facts. You don't vacillate about whether it rained yesterday. Vacillation is specifically about decisions, choices, opinions, or commitments — things that require you to take a position.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Vacillation is a formal word. You'll see it more in writing — in newspapers, essays, literature, and formal speeches — than in casual conversation. In everyday talk, people are more likely to say someone "keeps going back and forth" or "can't make up their mind."

The word carries a tone of criticism or disapproval. Accusing a politician of vacillation, for example, is a serious charge — it means they are unreliable, that they shift their positions based on pressure or mood rather than firm principle, and that people cannot trust what they say or where they stand.

It can also describe an internal, private struggle — someone torn between two things in their own mind — without any external criticism implied. But even then, it suggests a kind of suffering: the exhaustion of not being able to resolve something.

These examples show you the word working in real contexts:

  • "The prime minister's vacillation on the climate bill frustrated members of his own party, who could never be sure where he stood."
  • "After months of vacillation, she finally accepted the job offer." (Here, the vacillation is over — the decision has been made.)
  • "His vacillation between loyalty to his friend and his own moral values made him miserable."
  • "The general's vacillation at a critical moment in the battle cost them the victory."
  • "Stop this vacillation — the deadline is tomorrow and we need an answer."

If you want to lock this word in your memory permanently, hold onto these three points:

  1. Back and forth, again and again — not a single pause, but a repeated swinging between positions.
  2. Decisions, not facts — it's always about choices, opinions, or commitments.
  3. A word of criticism — it implies weakness of will, unreliability, or an inability to commit.

Master these three points, and you have truly mastered vacillation.
